summary: This BCP document contains a template for a Certification Practice Statement for an organization in the RPKI, such as a resource allocation registry or an ISP. It helps them describe how they operate their certificate authority.

eli5.summary: A template is a fill-in-the-blanks form. This RFC gives the form that organizations use to explain how they run the system that proves who owns Internet addresses.

questions: how to write an rpki cps
what is a certification practice statement
subtitle: A fill-in-the-blanks Certification Practice Statement for organizations that run a CA in the RPKI.

tldr.problem: Organizations that issue certificates in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), such as registries and ISPs, must document their practices, and writing that document from scratch is error-prone.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC supplies template text, with places marked in angle brackets for organization-specific details. It follows the outline of RFC 3647 and complements the RPKI Certificate Policy in RFC 6484.
tldr.outcome: As a best current practice, organizations are expected to use the template instead of creating one from scratch. No one expects the resulting CPS to be published as an RFC.

facts.label: Certificate status service
facts.value: CRLs only; no OCSP or SCVP

today: RFC 7382 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 173) and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the template that complements the RPKI Certificate Policy in RFC 6484.

sections.title: What the Template Is and How to Use It
sections.content:
The RFC contains text meant to be used as a template, marked by <BEGIN TEMPLATE TEXT> and <END TEMPLATE TEXT>. It is for creating a Certification Practice Statement (CPS) for an organization that is part of the RPKI. The CPS specifies the practices a Certification Authority employs in issuing certificates.

To use it, extract the text between the delimiters and replace the instructions inside angle brackets with the required information. The template contains both text that SHOULD appear in all CPSs and places for organization-specific text.

There is no expectation that a CPS will be published as an RFC. The organization publishes it in a suitable way, for example on its web site. The template complements the Certificate Policy for the RPKI (RFC 6484) and is based on the framework in RFC 3647. Sections that did not apply to this PKI were omitted, but the RFC 3647 section numbering is kept to ease comparison.
sections.eli5: It is a form with blanks. You copy the form, fill in the blanks about your own organization, and post it so others can read how you work.

sections.title: The RPKI and Its Participants
sections.content:
The RPKI is designed to support validation of claims by current holders of Internet Number Resources (INRs): IPv4 addresses, IPv6 addresses and the identifiers used in inter-domain routing, currently BGP-4 Autonomous System Numbers. The PKI parallels the existing distribution hierarchy. IANA distributes resources to the five Regional Internet Registries (RIRs), National Internet Registries (NIRs) form an optional tier under some RIRs, and ISPs and network subscribers form further tiers.

The template defines the participants. Subscribers are organizations receiving INR allocations from the CA. Relying parties act in reliance on certificates or RPKI-signed objects, and may or may not be subscribers. No separate Registration Authority is needed, and the RA function MUST be provided by the same entity operating as a CA. The template suggests, as one approach, an offline CA that issues certificates only to the production CA, and a production CA that issues certificates to members.

Certificates are for authorization in support of validating claims of INR holdings. Any other use is prohibited, apart from uses consistent with that goal that RFC 6484 permits.
sections.eli5: The system works like a family tree of who gave which addresses to whom. Each group that hands addresses down also hands out the proof papers, and anyone who checks those papers is a relying party.

sections.title: Naming and Identity Checks
sections.content:
Each certificate subject is identified by an X.500 Distinguished Name made of a single Common Name with a value generated by the organization. A serialNumber attribute may optionally be added to tell apart successive certificates for the same entity. Subject names SHOULD NOT be meaningful, because the certificates are used for authorization and not to identify subjects. Anonymity is not a function of this PKI.

Certificates do not attest to the organizational or individual identity of subscribers. They are issued so that they accurately reflect the organization's own records of INR distribution. The template asks the organization to describe how it proves possession of the private key, how it matches requests to its subscriber database, and how it authenticates individuals who represent subscribers. It gives an optional Business PKI (BPKI) as an example of how to do this. The RPKI is neither intended nor designed to interoperate with any other PKI.
sections.eli5: The names on the certificates are like random ID numbers, not real names. What matters is that the certificate matches the registry's own list of who holds which addresses.

sections.title: The Certificate Life Cycle
sections.content:
The template walks through application, issuance, acceptance, renewal, re-key, modification and revocation. Any subscriber in good standing who holds INRs distributed by the organization may apply, and most certificates are issued as a side effect of normal INR distribution.

  • Renewal: based on expiration or a request. The new certificate overlaps the old one so coverage is uninterrupted, and it reuses the same public key unless the private key was reported compromised.
  • Re-key: only when a private key is compromised or lost, or its cryptographic lifetime ends.
  • Modification: used when the INR holdings or repository publication data change. The new certificate keeps the same public key and expiration date. If resources are removed, the old certificate is revoked and a new one issued.
  • Revocation: the subscriber or the organization may request it, and the subscriber must request it as soon as possible after the need is identified.

Relying parties are responsible for acquiring and checking the most recent scheduled CRL from the issuer. Each CRL carries a nextUpdate value, and a new CRL is published at or before that time. The organization does not support OCSP or SCVP and issues only CRLs.
sections.eli5: Certificates are like library cards. They get renewed before they run out, replaced if the card is lost, updated when your borrowing rights change, and cancelled when you should not have one any more.

sections.title: Publication, Facilities and Key Controls
sections.content:
Certificates, CRLs and RPKI-signed objects MUST be available for download by all relying parties. The organization publishes them to a repository that is part of a worldwide distributed system of RPKI repositories and that follows the structure in RFC 6481. The template asks for the access controls that protect the repository and for the publication time frames.

The physical, procedural and personnel controls in section 5 are mostly headings with instructions to describe controls commensurate with those used for managing INR distribution. The audit log section does list auditable events, such as access to CA equipment, certificate requests and revocations, posting to a repository, attempts to change audit data, key generation, software updates and clock adjustments.

For technical controls, key sizes and algorithms are as in RFC 6485, certificate and CRL profiles are in RFC 6487, and key changeover follows RFC 6489. Trust anchor keys are distributed out of band. CA private keys are generated in a cryptographic module and never leave it except encrypted for backup or transfer. No private key escrow is required, and the RPKI does not use time-stamping.
sections.eli5: The organization has to say where the public notice board is, who is allowed to post on it, how it guards its secret keys, and how it keeps a diary of what happens to the machines.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Business Matters
sections.content:
How far a relying party can trust a certificate depends on the practices used to authenticate the subject, the CA's operating policy and technical controls, and the stated responsibilities and liability terms. The template is a framework for the technical, procedural, personnel and physical security aspects of CAs, RAs, repositories, subscribers and relying party cryptographic modules.

Section 9 of the template covers optional business and legal matters such as fees, insurance, confidentiality, privacy, warranties, liability, term and termination, amendments, dispute resolution and governing law. The organization fills these in as appropriate, in a way commensurate with how it handles these matters for INR distribution. Section 8 asks it to list the audits and assessments used to secure its administration of INRs.
sections.eli5: How much you trust a certificate depends on how carefully the issuer works. The form makes the issuer write down how careful they are, and the legal parts like fees and blame are optional blanks.
